neighbours.label: precaution scenarios: the point where a prepared helper gets to act if something goes wrong ('so they will ⟦know⟧…', 'paramedics ⟦can⟧ read it', 'the ranger ⟦will⟧ start a search'). Other side of the − pole's 'react/respond quickly'
fire: Give the school a list of your child's allergies, so the nurse will know what to do if there is a reaction.
Tape your emergency contacts inside the front door; if you fall, the ambulance crew can call your family at once.
Tell the lifeguard that your son is a weak swimmer, so she can keep an eye on him if the waves pick up.
Register your route with the harbour office; if the boat is overdue, the coastguard will send out a launch.
Keep a card in your wallet that lists your medicines, so doctors can check it if you are brought in unconscious.
Show a colleague where the inhaler is kept; if you have an attack, he will be able to fetch it for you.
Leave your itinerary with a friend, and if you have not phoned by Sunday she will alert the mountain rescue team.
Mark the gas shut-off valve with red paint, so that in a leak the fire crew can find it and close it.
quiet: Give the school a list of your child's favourite books, and the librarian may order some of them for next term.
Tape your shopping list inside the front door; the ambulance station down the road was repainted last spring.
The lifeguard said that her son is a strong swimmer and that the waves were small all afternoon.
The harbour office is open until six, and the coastguard museum next door shows old launches and lamps.
Keep a card in your wallet that lists your loyalty points; doctors and nurses get a discount at the cafe.
A colleague showed me where the coffee is kept; he drinks about four cups before lunch every day.
My friend spent Sunday reading about the history of the mountain rescue team and its first volunteers.
The gas company painted its vans red last year, and the fire crew thought the colour looked familiar.
